sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: JSON and HTTP are the first things every Go backend developer touches. Fresher interviews almost always include 'show me how you'd build a simple HTTP endpoint that accepts and returns JSON', and this module gives you everything needed to answer that question completely. Understanding struct tags, the silent-ignore of unexported fields, and the must-close-response-body pattern separates a candidate who has shipped Go services from one who has only done tutorials.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Three rules that cover most JSON/HTTP gotchas:

- **Unexported fields are silently ignored by `encoding/json`.** If your struct field starts with a lowercase letter, `json.Marshal` will not include it and `json.Unmarshal` will not populate it — with no error. This is a frequent bug in Go JSON code.
- **Always close the response body.** `resp, err := http.Get(url)` — if err is nil, `resp.Body` must be closed with `defer resp.Body.Close()`, even if you do not read the body. Not closing leaks the underlying TCP connection.
- **The handler signature is the contract.** `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)` — `w` is where you write the response, `r` is the incoming request. This signature is fixed; the router registers handlers that match it.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **json.Marshal / json.Unmarshal** — `json.Marshal(v)` returns `([]byte, error)`; `json.Unmarshal(data, &v)` populates v; unexported fields are silently ignored
- **JSON struct tags** — `` `json:"field_name"` `` sets the JSON key; `` `json:"-"` `` excludes the field; `` `json:"name,omitempty"` `` omits the field if it is the zero value
- **json.omitempty** — omits the field from JSON output if it is empty (zero value for the type: `0`, `false`, `""`, `nil`); useful for optional API fields
- **json.Number and interface{}** — by default, JSON numbers unmarshal to `float64` when the target is `interface{}`; use `json.Decoder.UseNumber()` to get `json.Number` instead, preserving large integer precision
- **http.Get and http.Post** — `resp, err := http.Get(url)`; always `defer resp.Body.Close()` after nil error check; `http.Post(url, "application/json", body)` for POST
- **Reading response body** — `data, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` reads the entire body to `[]byte`; then `json.Unmarshal(data, &target)` to decode
- **HTTP server basics** — `http.HandleFunc("/path", handler)` registers a handler; `http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)` starts the server; `nil` uses the default ServeMux

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Unexported field silently ignored** — `type User struct { name string }` will marshal to `{}`, not `{"name":"Alice"}`. The field must be `Name string` (capitalised). This is one of the most common Go JSON bugs.
- **Not closing response body** — every Go HTTP client question should include `defer resp.Body.Close()`. Candidates who omit it signal they have not shipped real Go code.
- **`json.NewDecoder` vs `json.Unmarshal`** — for HTTP handlers, `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v)` is preferred over reading the whole body first; it streams rather than buffering the entire request.
- **Setting Content-Type before WriteHeader** — `w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")` must come before `w.WriteHeader(200)`. Once `WriteHeader` is called (or the first `Write`), headers are frozen and further `Set` calls are silently ignored.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"For JSON in Go I use `encoding/json` — struct fields need to be exported and I control the JSON key with struct tags like `` `json:"user_id,omitempty"` ``. For HTTP clients I always `defer resp.Body.Close()` after checking the error, to prevent leaking connections. For HTTP servers I register handlers with `http.HandleFunc` using the `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)` signature, set headers before calling `WriteHeader`, and use `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(&v)` to stream the JSON response directly to the writer."*
